story.title: Supreme Court Allows Trump Administration to Use Federal Voter Eligibility Database Temporarily
story.summary: The Supreme Court has temporarily lifted restrictions on a federal voter eligibility database, allowing the Trump administration to use it ahead of the upcoming elections. This decision, made in a 6-3 ruling, supports the administration's efforts to verify voter citizenship status and potentially purge noncitizens from voter rolls. Critics have raised concerns about privacy and the implications of such actions on voter access.

explore_lenses.label: What changed in the SAVE system?
explore_lenses.title: The stay revives expanded search tools
explore_lenses.summary: The Court temporarily restored DHS’s revised SAVE system while the case proceeds. The dispute concerns 2025 changes that made voter-list checks broader and easier to run, not the original SAVE program in general.

claims.text: The Supreme Court granted the administration emergency relief from the June 2026 district-court ruling, pausing that ruling for now in a 6-3 decision.

According to the district court, the 2025 overhaul added natural-born-citizen records, enabled access to Social Security Administration records, including Social Security numbers, and allowed bulk searches by SAVE users.

Texas told the Supreme Court that the revised system allowed Social Security-number searches, bulk uploads, and no-fee searches; it said those changes let the state screen its statewide voter list more quickly and cheaply.

explore_lenses.label: Who could be affected by resumed checks?
explore_lenses.title: States regain a screening tool; voters may face follow-up
explore_lenses.summary: State and local election officials can again use the modified federal system to flag registrations for citizenship-related review. A SAVE response is not itself a voter-roll removal, but it can trigger state procedures that vary by jurisdiction.

claims.text: The Supreme Court said the lower-court order hindered federal assistance to state and local agencies administering the 2026 midterm elections.

Texas stated that SAVE does not definitively declare a person to be a noncitizen and that, under Texas law, voters identified as potentially ineligible are notified and given an opportunity to provide citizenship proof before cancellation.

The district court found that some plaintiffs’ members had been identified by SAVE as noncitizens and had registrations canceled, and it concluded that the revised system’s data could produce false identifications.

explore_lenses.label: What do Texas and the challengers argue?
explore_lenses.title: Accuracy and speed versus privacy and error risk
explore_lenses.summary: Texas and the federal government argue the revised system helps states meet voter-list maintenance duties. The League of Women Voters, EPIC, and allied local officials argue that combining and disclosing federal records created privacy violations and risks wrongful challenges to eligible voters.

claims.text: Texas argued that federal law requires DHS to respond to state and local government requests to verify citizenship or immigration status, and that the revised system enhanced Texas’s ability to maintain accurate rolls.
The district court held that the revised system and related notices violated the Social Security Act, Privacy Act, and Administrative Procedure Act, citing disclosure and procedural defects.

The Supreme Court’s unsigned emergency order said the challengers’ legal claims likely lacked merit and that the administration was likely to prevail over the district court’s ruling; Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson dissented.

story_report.summary: The Supreme Court, by a 6-3 vote, temporarily allowed the Trump administration to use a revamped federal database to help state and local officials verify voter citizenship. The emergency order pauses a June 2026 district-court ruling that had restricted the system, allowing its use during administration of the 2026 midterm elections while the underlying legal challenge continues. The Court said the lower-court order hindered federal assistance to election agencies.

sections.heading: SAVE Database Changes Expand Searches
sections.body: According to the district court, the 2025 overhaul of the SAVE system added natural-born-citizen records and access to Social Security Administration records, including Social Security numbers. It also enabled bulk searches by SAVE users. Texas said the revised system permits Social Security-number searches, bulk uploads and no-fee searches, allowing the state to screen its statewide voter list more quickly and cheaply.

sections.heading: Voter Database Legality Remains Contested
sections.body: The district court held that the revised system and related notices violated the Social Security Act, Privacy Act and Administrative Procedure Act, citing disclosure and procedural defects. It also found that some members of the plaintiff organizations had been identified as noncitizens through SAVE and had their registrations canceled, concluding that the system’s data could generate false identifications. Texas said SAVE does not conclusively determine that a person is a noncitizen and that state law provides notice and an opportunity to submit citizenship proof before cancellation.

sections.heading: Emergency Order Leaves Merits Unresolved
sections.body: In its unsigned order, the Supreme Court said the challengers’ claims likely lacked merit and that the administration was likely to prevail against the district-court ruling. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. The stay is temporary and does not finally determine whether the SAVE changes comply with the cited federal laws or what final remedy could apply.

unresolved.text: It remains unknown how many voters, if any, may be flagged or removed while the stay is in effect, because outcomes depend on which jurisdictions use the system and on their separate notice-and-review procedures.

related_stories.title: Protests Erupt in India Demanding Resignation of Election Chief
related_stories.summary: A youth group known as the 'Cockroach' movement has threatened to resume mass protests unless Gyanesh Kumar resigns as head of India's election commission. This demand follows allegations of election rigging, which have also prompted opposition parties, including Congress, to join the protests. Police have responded with tear gas to disperse demonstrators.

related_stories.title: Xi Jinping Concludes US Visit with National Archives Tour
related_stories.summary: Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded his three-day state visit to the United States with a tour of the National Archives, accompanied by President Donald Trump. The visit included viewing significant documents such as the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution. The trip has faced criticism for lacking substantive discussions.

related_stories.title: Media Outlets Return to White House Following Court Order, Denied Access to State Dinner
related_stories.summary: Several media outlets, including CNN and MS NOW, returned to the White House after a judge ordered the restoration of their press passes, which had been revoked by the Trump administration. However, reporters from these outlets were denied access to cover the arrival of Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state dinner, despite the court ruling.

related_stories.title: Iran Unveils 7-Day Plan to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz
related_stories.summary: Iran has proposed a seven-day plan aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The proposal comes as the Iranian government seeks to negotiate a deal with the U.S. before the upcoming midterm elections in November, amid rising fuel prices that are putting pressure on the U.S. administration.
